title: Linear Programming and the Graphical Method
subject: LIT 803
description: Twenty-five questions across easy, medium and hard on LP requirements, canonical and standard form, and the graphical method with the radio production example.

questions.prompt: How is linear programming described in Definition 1?
options: A method of storing data in tables
A way to count stock items
A technique to allocate scarce resources among competing activities in an optimal manner
questions.explanation: LP is an optimisation tool for limited resources.

questions.prompt: What does an LP model optimise?
options: A linear objective function subject to linear equality or inequality constraints
A curved objective with no limits
Only the cost of one resource
questions.explanation: This is Definition 2.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the five basic requirements for LP?
options: Linearity of the objective function and the constraints
questions.explanation: The others are a well-defined objective, alternative courses of action, inter-related variables and resource scarcity.

questions.prompt: What does a slack variable do?
options: It is subtracted from a ≥ constraint
It changes the objective into a minimum
It is added to a ≤ constraint to capture unused capacity
questions.explanation: For a ≤ constraint, aX + bY + s = c with s ≥ 0.

questions.prompt: What does a surplus variable do?
options: It is added to a ≤ constraint
It is subtracted from a ≥ constraint to absorb the excess over the minimum
questions.explanation: For a ≥ constraint, aX + bY − s = c with s ≥ 0.

questions.prompt: What is standard form?
options: A form where every constraint is ≤
A form in which all structural inequality constraints are converted into equalities
A form with no objective function
A form with only two variables
questions.explanation: Standard form is needed before running the Simplex algorithm.

questions.prompt: In canonical form, how are the constraints of a maximisation problem written?
options: As a mix of any signs
questions.explanation: For minimisation problems, all constraints are written as ≥.

questions.prompt: Which theorem says that the optimum of a graphical LP is at a corner of the feasible region?
questions.explanation: The vertex with the extreme value of Z is the optimal solution.

questions.prompt: In canonical form, how are the constraints of a minimisation problem written?
options: As a mix of any signs
questions.explanation: Maximisation uses ≤ and minimisation uses ≥.

questions.prompt: How is an unrestricted variable Xⱼ handled in standard form?
options: Make it equal to a slack variable
Replace it with Wⱼ − Sⱼ, where Wⱼ ≥ 0 and Sⱼ ≥ 0
questions.explanation: The difference of two non-negative variables can be positive or negative.

questions.prompt: How is the constraint X₁ + 4X₂ ≥ 8 written in standard form?
questions.explanation: A surplus variable is subtracted, and it has a zero coefficient in the objective.

questions.prompt: How is the constraint 2X₁ + X₂ ≤ 12 written in standard form?
questions.explanation: A slack variable is added, and it has a zero coefficient in the objective.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the graphical solution procedure?
options: Convert the inequality constraints to boundary line equations
questions.explanation: The steps are boundary lines, plotting, feasible region, corner coordinates, then evaluating Z.

questions.prompt: What is the iso-profit line method?
options: Plot only the constraint with the lowest profit
Shade the area outside the feasible region
Add the profit of every corner
Slide a line of constant Z parallel outward until it last touches the feasible region
questions.explanation: For a cost problem, the iso-cost line is used in the same way.

questions.prompt: Why does the feed mill model in Problem 2 use an equality for total weight?
options: Every constraint in an LP must be an equality
The batch must weigh exactly 600 kg
questions.explanation: The model is X₁ + X₂ + X₃ = 600, with X₁ ≥ 100 and X₂ ≤ 200.

questions.prompt: How does the constraint X₂ ≥ 0.40(X₁ + X₂ + X₃) look in the blade exercise after rearranging?
questions.explanation: Move 0.40(X₁ + X₂ + X₃) to the left: X₂ − 0.4X₁ − 0.4X₂ − 0.4X₃ = −0.4X₁ + 0.6X₂ − 0.4X₃.

questions.prompt: In the mining shipping problem, why does it not matter that supply is written as ≤ and demand as ≥?
options: Supply is always larger than demand
Demand constraints are ignored by the solver
Total supply (900 kg) equals total demand (900 kg), so every constraint is effectively an equality

questions.prompt: In the worked example Max Z = X₁ + 2X₂ with X₁ + X₂ ≤ 4, X₁ ≥ 1 and X₁ − X₂ ≤ 2, which vertex is optimal and what is Z?
questions.explanation: The corner values are 7, 5, 2 and 1, and the largest is at A.

questions.prompt: In the same example, if the problem were to minimise Z, which vertex would give the smallest value?
questions.explanation: B has Z = 5, which is neither the maximum nor the minimum. The smallest value is at D.

questions.prompt: In the radio example, how is vertex C found, and what are its coordinates?
options: The X₁ = 20 line meets assembly at (20, 48)
The manufacturing and assembly lines intersect at about (61.54, 23.08)
The X₂ = 10 line meets manufacturing at (72, 10)
The two minimum lines meet at (20, 10)
questions.explanation: Solving 5X₁ + 4X₂ = 400 and 6X₁ + 10X₂ = 600 gives X₁ = 61.54 and X₂ = 23.08.

questions.prompt: What is the optimal plan for Mr. Anyanwu's radio production?
options: 72 units of Model A and 10 units of Model B, with a profit of ₦2,250
61.54 units of Model A and 23.08 units of Model B, with a profit of ₦2,577.10
20 units of Model A and 10 units of Model B, with a profit of ₦950
20 units of Model A and 48 units of Model B, with a profit of ₦2,660
questions.explanation: D(20, 48) gives 25(20) + 45(48) = 2,660, the largest corner value.

questions.prompt: At the optimal radio plan D(20, 48), how many hours are idle in each department?
options: Manufacturing 108 hours idle, assembly 0 hours idle
Manufacturing 0 hours idle, assembly 108 hours idle
Manufacturing 292 hours idle, assembly 600 hours idle
questions.explanation: Manufacturing uses 5(20) + 4(48) = 292 of 400 hours. Assembly uses 6(20) + 10(48) = 600 of 600 hours, so it is the binding constraint.

questions.prompt: In the radio example, vertex B (72, 10) comes from which intersection?
questions.explanation: With X₂ = 10, 5X₁ + 40 = 400 gives X₁ = 72.

questions.prompt: Which set of properties does Definition 3 give for linear programming?
questions.explanation: LP is a deterministic framework, so all data are taken as certain.

questions.prompt: In Problem 1 (the three-product firm), which constraints show the sales commitments?
questions.explanation: The other constraints are the planning, milling and assembly hour limits.
